activity.title: Separating sending time from signal travel time
activity.learning_objective: Explain why changing cable length alone changes propagation delay but not transmission delay.
activity.rationale: Predict a change, then explain the reasoning for Transmission delay, prompted by recorded reasoning: “Both double. Transmission takes twice as long because the bits must be transmitted across twice the distance.”. Correct or contrary evidence is also retained for review.
activity.explanation:
Second, there is the amount of time it takes to transmit a unit of data.
This is a function of the network bandwidth and the size of the packet in
which the data is carried.

Propagation =  Distance/SpeedOfLight
   Transmit = Size/Bandwidth

where ``Distance`` is the length of the wire over which the data will
travel, ``SpeedOfLight`` is the effective speed of light over that wire,
``Size`` is the size of the packet, and ``Bandwidth`` is the bandwidth
at which the packet is transmitted.
activity.exercise_text: For each situation, predict transmission delay and propagation delay separately before reading the source excerpts. Explain which changed quantity matters for each delay and which quantities remain fixed. Then use the excerpts to check your reasoning and revise it if needed.

practice_questions.prompt_text: A sensor sends a packet over a single cable. The cable is replaced by a shorter cable with the same effective signal speed. Packet size and link transmission rate stay fixed. Predict whether each delay decreases, increases, or stays unchanged. Explain your predictions by identifying what determines each delay.

where ``Distance`` is the length of the wire over which the data will
travel, ``SpeedOfLight`` is the effective speed of light over that wire,
``Size`` is the size of the packet, and ``Bandwidth`` is the bandwidth
at which the packet is transmitted.

evidence_references.response_quote: Both double. Transmission takes twice as long because the bits must be transmitted across twice the distance.
On A, transmission and propagation are each 1 ms. On B, both are 3 ms, because transmitting across three times the distance takes three times as long.
More bits take longer to put onto the link, but the distance and propagation speed stay the same.
Only propagation changes with the distance.
Transmission delay is unchanged: the number of packet bits and the rate at which they enter the link are unchanged. Propagation delay doubles because distance doubles at the same propagation speed.

concept.title: Transmission delay
objectives: Explain transmission delay as the time needed to place a packet's bits onto the link at its given rate.
Use transmission delay = packet size in bits / link rate in bits per second.
Predict the effect of changing packet size or link rate while holding other relevant quantities fixed.
Explain why changing cable length alone changes propagation delay but not transmission delay.
boundaries: Use the stated effective transmission rate; do not substitute measured application throughput without an explicit instruction.
Use a single link with stated assumptions; do not infer extra hops when cable length changes.
Do not assess the source's simplifying one-bit remark in P08.

related_concepts.title: Bandwidth and measured throughput
objectives: Describe link bandwidth or data rate in bits per second and measured throughput as actual observed performance.
Calculate an observed data-transfer rate from a stated bit count and elapsed time.
Explain why a link's available data rate need not equal measured throughput.
Recognize that small exchanges and large transfers can emphasize different performance limits.
boundaries: Frequency-domain bandwidth in hertz is contextual reading, not an assessed objective.
Do not require explanations involving unassigned transport protocols, congestion-control algorithms, or detailed overhead accounting.
Application examples compare the stated conditions only; neither latency nor bandwidth always dominates.

related_concepts.title: Propagation delay
objectives: Explain propagation delay as signal travel time along a link.
Use propagation delay = cable length / effective signal speed in that medium.
Predict effects of changing distance or propagation speed while stating what remains fixed.
Distinguish propagation delay from effects of packet size and link data rate on transmission delay.
boundaries: Use the supplied signal speed; students need not memorize the medium-specific values.
Propagation delay is not the time until an entire packet finishes arriving; transmission contributes to whole-packet delivery.
No claims about the engineering feasibility of changing one parameter independently are assessed.

related_concepts.title: Queuing delay and total latency
objectives: Identify time a packet waits inside a switch before forwarding as queuing delay.
Distinguish waiting from transmission and propagation.
Add supplied propagation, transmission, and queue components in the source's simplified latency model.
Find an unknown queue component from a supplied total and the other two components.
boundaries: Every numerical queue duration is supplied directly or follows by subtraction from supplied component totals.
Do not assess queue distributions, traffic intensity, arrival rates, utilization, packet loss, or scheduling theory.
The simplified three-component model is assumed in the questions; do not imply it is exhaustive for every real network.

question.prompt_text: A single cable becomes twice as long. Packet size, link transmission rate, and propagation speed stay unchanged. What happens to transmission delay and propagation delay? Explain why.

rubric.answer_guidance: Transmission delay is unchanged because it is packet size divided by transmission rate, both fixed. Propagation delay doubles because it is cable length divided by propagation speed, and only cable length doubles.
criteria: Identify packet size and transmission rate as the determinants of transmission delay.
Identify cable length and propagation speed as the determinants of propagation delay.
Apply the stated controlled change to both quantities.
acceptable_variations: The time to put the packet onto the cable stays the same; its signal travel time doubles.
Verbal proportional reasoning is sufficient; equations are optional.
rubric.partial_credit_guidance: One correct effect with the other missing or wrong is partial. Both effects correct without explanation are partial and need a brief reasoning probe. If the student uses transmission to mean total delivery, clarify terminology before assigning a misconception hypothesis.

sources.text:
While you can talk about the bandwidth of the network as a whole,
sometimes you want to be more precise, focusing, for example, on the
bandwidth of a single physical link or of a logical process-to-process
channel. At the physical level, bandwidth is constantly improving, with
no end in sight. Intuitively, if you think of a second of time as a
distance you could measure with a ruler and bandwidth as how many bits
fit in that distance, then you can think of each bit as a pulse of some
width. For example, each bit on a 1-Mbps link is 1 μs wide, while each
bit on a 2-Mbps link is 0.5 μs wide, as illustrated in :numref:`Figure
%s <fig-bit-width>`. The more sophisticated the transmitting and receiving
technology, the narrower each bit can become and, thus, the higher the
bandwidth. For logical process-to-process channels, bandwidth is also
influenced by other factors, including how many times the software that
implements the channel has to handle, and possibly transform, each bit
of data.

We often think of latency as having three components. First, there is
the speed-of-light propagation delay. This delay occurs because nothing,
including a bit on a wire, can travel faster than the speed of light. If
you know the distance between two points, you can calculate the
speed-of-light latency, although you have to be careful because light
travels across different media at different speeds: It travels at
3.0 × 10\ :sup:`8` m/s in a vacuum, 2.3 × 10\ :sup:`8` m/s
in a copper cable, and 2.0 × 10\ :sup:`8` m/s in an optical fiber.
Second, there is the amount of time it takes to transmit a unit of data.
This is a function of the network bandwidth and the size of the packet in
which the data is carried. Third, there may be queuing delays inside the
network, since packet switches generally need to store packets for some
time before forwarding them on an outbound link. So, we could define the
total latency as

::

   Latency = Propagation + Transmit + Queue
   Propagation =  Distance/SpeedOfLight
   Transmit = Size/Bandwidth

where ``Distance`` is the length of the wire over which the data will
travel, ``SpeedOfLight`` is the effective speed of light over that wire,
``Size`` is the size of the packet, and ``Bandwidth`` is the bandwidth
at which the packet is transmitted. Note that if the message contains
only one bit and we are talking about a single link (as opposed to a
whole network), then the ``Transmit`` and ``Queue`` terms are not
relevant, and latency corresponds to the propagation delay only.
